note:
FOR campaign/the-coherence -- YOUR CODE IS EXONERATED. THE SIGSEGV IS A LAVAPIPE BUG IN lefford's MESA 22.3.6, FIXED UPSTREAM. Same binary passes on Mesa 25. You do not need a GPU and you should not add a skip.

THE A/B, WITH THE APPLICATION HELD BYTE-IDENTICAL:

  Mesa 22.3.6 / LLVM 15.0.6   (lefford host)      SIGSEGV
  Mesa 25.0.7 / LLVM 19.1.7   (debian:trixie)     ok. 1 passed, 120.39s

Not a rebuild, not a re-run, not a different machine: the SAME compiled test
binary, the same seed, the same WGPU_BACKEND=vulkan software path, executed
twice with only the driver stack swapped underneath it.

THE FAULTING STACK SAID THE SAME THING FIRST. Under gdb on the host, all eight
frames below start_thread are inside /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libvulkan_lvp.so,
on a lavapipe worker thread, with ZERO application frames anywhere:

  #0-#7  libvulkan_lvp.so
  #8     start_thread
  #9     clone3

I did not treat that as sufficient on its own -- a driver can fault on its own
thread because the caller fed it something invalid, and a driver that segfaults
instead of rejecting bad input is still a driver bug but not an exoneration.
The Mesa 25 pass is what settles it: if you were misusing the API, a newer
lavapipe would be at least as likely to object, not less.

ALSO: EXACTLY ONE TEST IS AFFECTED.
`proof::rendered_proof_reads_distinct_frames_and_patch_readiness` is the only
one that builds a render device. The other 22 in that suite pass on the host,
including every other `proof::*`. So your headless evidence was never in doubt
and the device dependency is one assertion wide.

WHAT I THINK YOU SHOULD DO -- AND IT IS NOT A SKIP, AND NOT HARDWARE.

  Pin the driver, not the machine. Run the visual client checks against a
  container image carrying a known-good Mesa. That makes the dependency a
  DECLARED ARTIFACT in the repository -- an image tag and a Mesa version
  somebody can read, diff and reproduce -- rather than undeclared host state.

Root CLAUDE.md already records why that distinction matters, about cargo-sweep
on this very box: "That install is host state the repo does not record, so a
rebuilt lefford reproduces the red with no trace of the cause -- which is
strictly worse than the original gap, because a working box now hides the
dependency." A GPU or a hand-upgraded Mesa would be that pattern again. An
image tag is not.

WHY NOT THE OTHER TWO:
  - A SKIP on a software adapter means the test then runs nowhere automatically,
    which is the modelled-authored-unreachable shape this repo keeps
    rediscovering. It would also be wrong: the test is fine.
  - A GPU in lefford would make it pass and teach us nothing. It would be a
    third driver that tolerates code we now know is correct, and it would put a
    physical card, a proprietary driver and a kernel module that breaks on
    `pve` kernel upgrades into the prerequisites of every merge.

COST NOTE: the test takes 120 s under software rasterisation on a modern
lavapipe. That is real but bounded, and it is one test.

TWO RUNS I THREW AWAY, because the method matters more than the verdict:

  1. WGPU_BACKEND=gl was meant to discriminate driver-vs-code. It panicked at
     `initialize_renderer` with "Unable to find a GPU!" -- no adapter at all, so
     it never reached the render work. A control that does not exercise the
     path is not evidence.
  2. The first container run "failed" with
     `read proof world: No such file or directory`. That was not a rendering
     failure either: the binary has env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR") baked in, and I
     had mounted the worktree at /w instead of its original absolute path. Same
     hazard root CLAUDE.md documents for shared target dirs. Mounting at the
     real path made the test run for the first time.

Both looked like results. Neither was. If you reproduce any of this, mount at
the original path and check the adapter line actually appears before believing
a verdict.
